result.summary: Pausanias travels from Acraephnium through the Copaic lake region of Boeotia, describing Copae, Olmones, Hyettus, Cyrtones and Corsea. He notes temples, statues, a flood that destroyed old towns, and the fine eels of the lake.

scenes.title: Lake Cephisis and Copae
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the plain Athamantium, the lake fed by the Cephisus, and the temples at Copae. He tells of the flooded towns and the excellent eels.

scenes.title: Olmones and Hyettus
scenes.summary: Pausanias passes Olmones and reaches Hyettus, where Hercules heals the sick through a statue of rude stone.

scenes.title: Cyrtones, Corsea and Halae
scenes.summary: He describes the hill town Cyrtones with its sanctuaries, then Corsea, its grove with a Hermes statue, and the coast at Halae.

analysis.text: Pausanias catalogues local cults, statues and traditions, showing how religion was tied to place in Boeotia.
The ancient statue of rude stone and the temple of Serapis show both archaic worship and newer cults in Roman-era Greece.

fun_facts.text: Lake Copais was drained in antiquity and again in the 1880s, and is now farmland.

language_notes.text: Homer's Catalogue of the ships (Iliad, Book 2) lists the Greek contingents at Troy, naming Boeotian towns including Copae.
This Athenae and Eleusis are Boeotian towns, not the famous Attic ones; they were said to have been lost to the lake's flooding.
A stade is a Greek unit of distance, roughly 180–200 metres.
Pausanias refers ahead to his account of Orchomenus, where he will give the legends of Hyettus and Olmus.
"Not artistic, but made of rude stone" means an unworked, unshaped stone, kept as an ancient cult object.
"In a standing picture" is an awkward rendering; it likely means the statues stand upright, though the original sense is unclear.
Holm-oaks are evergreen oaks with glossy, often prickly leaves, common around the Mediterranean.

context_notes.text: Serapis was a Greco-Egyptian god promoted under the Ptolemies, so his temple here shows Egyptian cults reaching Boeotia.
Hercules was widely worshipped as a healer and protector, so sick pilgrims seeking cures at his shrine is not surprising.
Halae lay on the Boeotian coast facing the Euboean strait, near the Locrian border.

literary_notes.text: "The Boeotians say" distances the narrator from the flood story, marking it as local tradition rather than his own claim.
Pausanias' aside on the eels shows his curiosity about local life and his taste for practical detail alongside antiquities.
